scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The ula is an ancient Tongan group dance whose antiquity is attested by early European navigators, including Captain James Cook, who recorded it during eighteenth-century voyages to the Friendly Islands.
Prior to the arrival of Christianity, the ula stood as Tonga's primary dance performed by women.

Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Traditionally scheduled after the ʻotuhaka, the ula functions as a formal group dance expressing royal and communal poetry through synchronized gesture.
Before Christian missionization transformed Tongan social aesthetics, it served as the foremost female dance expression across the kingdom.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed almost exclusively by girls, with boys joining only on rare occasions.

The hallmark structure that gives the dance its alternate name—fahaʻi-ula, or split dance—lies in its entrance: the ensemble divides into two or more contingents, with one half entering from the left and the other from the right.
The groups converge in the center of the performance space, merging into one or more horizontal rows.
Watch for Fahaʻi entry, Haka hand shaping.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (OsSEe6d1GCs)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Bilateral entrance from stage left and stage right, converging at the center into one or more parallel lines

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Performers dress in attire identical in structure to that worn for the tauʻolunga, though red dress is distinctly favored and most popular for the ula.
The setting typically places the dance within a larger ceremonial order: traditionally, the ula is performed immediately after an ʻotuhaka.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Captain James Cook noted and reported the dance during his early European explorations of Tonga.
Historic poetic texts linked to the dance explicitly memorialize noble figures such as Tuʻi Vaea ('Laulau tuʻi Vaea ē, / Vaea lau mānaʻia').
The ula is an ancestral group dance from which the widely known Tongan tauʻolunga developed as a direct descendant, ultimately replacing the ula as the kingdom's preeminent female dance.

scenes.title: Family tree

Ula is child of tauʻolunga: The tauʻolunga is a direct descendant of the ula and largely replaced it in modern popularity.

narration: Avoid exaggerated hip movement or loose upper-body swaying, which were explicitly banned by royal reforms in favor of conservative stiffness
